sentence: "She would visit every summer" describes a repeated past habit, which French renders with the imperfect (elle rendait visite chaque été), not the conditional, despite the English wording looking identical to a hypothetical "would." The hypothetical and future-of-the-past senses of "would" can map onto the conditionnel; the habitual-past sense doesn\'t, which is the exact same trap [Spanish\'s own conditional entry describes](/spanish-conditional-tense/) for that language\'s identical false-friend problem with "would."
note: Current Spanish conditional target distinguishes hypothetical/future-of-past would from past habitual would rendered imperfect; exact restricted false-friend comparison.
target_quote: 'English "would" is genuinely ambiguous, and that ambiguity is exactly what trips up learners translating into Spanish. "She would visit every summer" describes a repeated habit in the past (no hypothesis involved, nothing conditional about it), and that sentence takes the Spanish imperfect: *visitaba cada verano*. "She would visit if she had the time" is a hypothetical conditional, contingent on having the time, and that one takes the conditional: *visitaría si tuviera tiempo*. These examples illustrate one contrast, without exhausting the uses of *cantaría, visitaría,* and *comería*. For the first, plain habitual "would," Spanish wants [the imperfect](/preterite-vs-imperfect/) instead. For this plain past habit, visitaba gives the intended meaning; visitaría would invite a conditional or future-from-past reading instead.',
